findings.consequent: differential intake and recovery responses to natural vs urban environments

The physiological data were obtained at different times than ZIPERS self-ratings, leading to few significant correlations between the ZIPERS self-ratings and physiological results. (p. 218, 221)
Temporal non-congruence of the different measurement modes. (p. 221)
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated stress recovery in 120 subjects exposed to either natural or urban audiovisual environments after a stressful movie. Findings consistently showed that exposure to natural settings led to faster and more complete physiological (skin conductance, muscle tension, pulse transit time) and psychological (reduced fear, anger, increased positive affect) stress recovery compared to urban settings. Natural environments also elicited higher and sustained attention (heart rate deceleration), potentially involving the parasympathetic nervous system, while urban settings led to heart rate acceleration. The study concluded that content differences (natural vs. human-made properties) were decisive for recovery, largely contradicting arousal theory's predictions about stimulation levels. Limitations include the inability to precisely disentangle sympathetic/parasympathetic influences and the generalizability to longer-term, active nature experiences.

environmental_features: scenes of natural environments (e.g., forests, parks, water features, vegetation)
scenes of urban environments (e.g., city streets, buildings, traffic, concrete)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments elicits positive affective responses and reduces physiological arousal, leading to faster and more complete stress recovery compared to urban environments.
Natural environments facilitate the restoration of directed attention, which is depleted by demanding cognitive tasks, through qualities like fascination, being away, extent, and compatibility.

mechanism_chain.description: The mechanism posits that natural environments trigger an immediate, involuntary positive affective response and a reduction in physiological stress indicators, leading to faster recovery from psychological stress.

steps.from_construct: Visual exposure to natural elements (e.g., vegetation, water)
steps.to_construct: Elicitation of positive affect (e.g., pleasantness, calm) and reduction of negative affect (e.g., fear, anger)

steps.from_construct: Reduced negative affect and increased positive affect
steps.to_construct: Reduction in physiological arousal (e.g., heart rate, blood pressure, muscle tension)
